question: A shared Blob Storage account holds data for two business units in separate containers. Both units must keep server-side encryption, but each needs a distinct customer-managed encryption key and independent rotation ownership without creating another account. Which design meets the key-boundary requirement?

answerChoices.text: Use one account-scoped Microsoft-managed key and rotate each container name.
Enable infrastructure encryption and assign a different infrastructure key per container.
Send a customer-provided key only when reading each container listing.
Use separate encryption scopes with customer-managed keys for the containers.

explanation: Encryption scopes provide container or blob key boundaries within one account and can use customer-managed keys.
deepExplanation: The required boundary is narrower than the default account-wide encryption key. Customer-managed keys are maintained in Key Vault or Managed HSM, while infrastructure encryption uses its own Microsoft-managed key. An encryption boundary does not replace data-access authorization.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: A single Microsoft-managed account key does not provide independently customer-managed container keys.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Infrastructure encryption uses Microsoft-managed keys rather than customer-selected container-specific infrastructure keys.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: Customer-provided keys are supplied on blob data operations; a listing-only change does not establish container encryption scopes.

subskill: Implement and configure security for storage accounts
documentationTitles: Azure Storage encryption for data at rest
verificationNotes: Checked the scope paragraph, key-management table and infrastructure paragraph independently. Separate CMK scopes satisfy the one-account, container-boundary and ownership constraints; Key Vault/Managed HSM is correctly stated in the explanation. This is a distinct key-scope decision from 037, not a second encryption-layer question. Advanced difficulty is only partially convincing, and renaming a container is a weak alternative; the rubric records both deductions.
confidenceReason: Container/blob scope and customer-managed key support are explicit, rather than inferred from account-level encryption.

question: A supported Azure resource cannot be isolated with a VNet or IP rule. It belongs to a different subscription but the same tenant as a locked-down storage account. The resource instance needs read-only data access. Which two controls must the engineer combine? Select two.

answerChoices.text: A resource instance network rule for that resource.
An Azure role assignment granting the required data operations.
A move into the storage account subscription as a prerequisite.
An IP-scoped SAS that overrides the account network deny.

explanation: Use a resource instance network rule for network admission and an appropriate role assignment for read access.
deepExplanation: Resource instance rules permit supported resources in the same tenant, including another subscription. They do not themselves select which data operations the resource may perform; its role assignments determine those operations.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: The documented tenant boundary does not require the resource and storage account to share a subscription.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: A SAS can constrain a token holder but cannot override the storage firewall.

documentationTitles: Azure Storage firewall rules and network access control
verificationNotes: Evaluated network admission and data permission as two distinct controls, without deriving the pair from the author key. Same tenant, supported resource and cross-subscription placement are explicit prerequisites. The pronouns identify that resource unambiguously. The item is a configuration decision rather than a rich troubleshooting exercise; difficulty scores 1. Its core same-tenant/resource-instance boundary differs from the source-IP transition in 038 and SAS-only proposal in 040.
confidenceReason: Both the cross-subscription allowance and role-determined operations are stated together in the resource-instance section.

question: A legacy integration must continue using service SAS tokens. Several tokens for one blob container must be revocable together without rotating the account key or disrupting unrelated SAS grants. The tokens have not yet been issued. Which issuance design supports that control?

answerChoices.text: Associate those service SAS tokens with a dedicated stored access policy.
Issue account SAS tokens with the same container policy identifier.
Issue ad hoc service SAS tokens and maintain only an external token list.
Associate user delegation SAS tokens with a stored access policy.

explanation: A stored access policy can manage and revoke the permissions of the associated service SAS tokens without key rotation.
deepExplanation: The policy association must be part of the issuance design. Account SAS and user delegation SAS are ad hoc and do not support stored access policies. Merely tracking ad hoc tokens externally does not create a server-side revocation control.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Account SAS does not support a stored access policy.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: An external list does not bind the ad hoc tokens to a revocable storage policy.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: User delegation SAS does not support stored access policies and would also change the required SAS type.

question: A SQL Server Contributor provisions a logical server and configures its Entra administrator but cannot enable Entra-only authentication. The organization wants security-control management separated from routine server provisioning. Which built-in assignment should go to the security operator for this control?

answerChoices.text: SQL Security Manager at the appropriate scope.
SQL Server Contributor again, through a second group.
SQL Managed Instance Contributor on the logical server.
Only database CONTROL permission, with no Azure management assignment.

explanation: SQL Security Manager includes management of Entra-only authentication; SQL Server Contributor does not.
deepExplanation: The configured Entra administrator satisfies a prerequisite but does not give the provisioning role the missing Azure management action. The documented separation allows security operators to manage this control independently of server provisioning.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Duplicating the same role does not add its excluded Entra-only management permission.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: SQL Managed Instance Contributor also lacks permission to enable or disable this feature.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: Database permission does not supply the Azure resource management action for this server-level control.

question: SQL Database auditing to a storage account worked until outbound networking restrictions were introduced on the logical server. Storage authorization is unchanged, but the audit storage endpoint is absent from the outbound allowlist. Which two steps address the documented recovery procedure? Select two.

answerChoices.text: Disable database authentication so audit traffic bypasses outbound restrictions.
Allowlist the auditing storage account FQDNs.
Re-save the auditing configuration after allowing the destination.
Increase the audit statement character limit in the database.

explanation: Allow the audit storage destination FQDNs and then re-save the auditing configuration.
deepExplanation: Audit output needs an allowed outbound destination as well as valid storage authorization. The documentation explicitly calls for re-saving the audit settings after adding the destination so event flow resumes.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Database authentication settings do not supply outbound network access to the audit destination.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: Statement truncation is unrelated to a blocked destination, and this is not the documented recovery operation.

question: A Virtual WAN has Hub East with Azure Firewall and an Internet Traffic routing policy. Hub West has no security appliance or routing policies. A design assumes West-connected spokes can use East’s firewall for internet egress merely through inter-hub connectivity. What invalidates this assumption?

answerChoices.text: The default route is not propagated between hubs, so this configuration does not provide that remote-hub internet path.
Internet policy advertises only individual website prefixes, not a default route.
Internet Traffic routing policies apply only to ExpressRoute branches, never VNet connections.
A Private Traffic policy in East automatically propagates its internet default route to West.

explanation: The routing-intent design does not propagate the default route across hubs.
deepExplanation: Internet policy sends connected spokes and branches to the local security solution. A hub lacking that configured local path cannot assume it inherits another hub’s internet egress simply because private inter-hub connectivity exists.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Internet routing policy advertises a 0.0.0.0/0 default route to connected resources.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: The documented Internet policy includes VNet connections and multiple branch types.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: A Private policy does not make the default route propagate between hubs.

question: A conventional load-balancer-backed Private Link service must accept connection requests from two partner subscriptions. One partner is preapproved; the other requires manual security approval. Which combination preserves this distinction?

answerChoices.text: Put both subscriptions in auto-approval and rely on visibility for manual review.
Share the alias and assume every visible requester is automatically approved.
Include both subscriptions in visibility, but only the preapproved subscription in auto-approval.
Put the manual-review subscription outside visibility and approve it after it connects.

explanation: Visibility controls who can request a connection; auto-approval controls which visible subscriptions are approved without manual action.
deepExplanation: The auto-approval set is a subset of the visibility set. The second partner can submit a pending request but cannot send service traffic until the provider approves it. Sharing an alias alone is not approval.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: Putting both partners in auto-approval removes the required manual approval distinction.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Visible subscriptions not in auto-approval still require provider action.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: Excluding the partner from visibility prevents the intended request path rather than creating a manual-approval workflow.

question: An MSSP calls a customer-tenant incident playbook from an automation rule created while signed into the provider tenant. The customer already grants its Sentinel service account permission on the playbook resource group. The existing Azure Lighthouse delegation covers the human operator but omits the provider-side service application. Which value belongs in principalId in the additional authorization entry?

answerChoices.text: The Object ID of the human operator in the provider tenant
The Object ID of Azure Security Insights under Microsoft Applications in the provider tenant
The directory tenant ID of the customer that owns the playbook
The Azure resource ID of the Logic App workflow in the customer tenant

explanation: Use the provider tenant’s Azure Security Insights application Object ID in the additional Azure Lighthouse authorization.
deepExplanation: The documented MSSP configuration requires authorization in both tenants. The customer-side playbook permission is already present here; the remaining provider-side step is to locate Azure Security Insights in Enterprise applications, filtered to Microsoft Applications, and add that application’s Object ID to the Lighthouse delegation with the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role. A human delegate, a tenant identifier and a workflow resource identifier are different objects and do not identify that service application.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.a: The operator is already delegated. The documented extra authorization is for Azure Security Insights, not another human assignment.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.c: The instructions require the Object ID of the service application, not the customer directory identifier.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: The workflow is the target resource; the documented principal is the provider-side service application.
